title: How To Handle Parents Who Complain About Their Child Being Held Accountable t-their-child-being-held-accountable/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin addresses a growing situation among SCM readers: parents who don't dispute their child's misbehavior but object to the consequence itself, often out of personal frustration that things aren't going as smoothly as they'd hoped for their child. He offers a three-step approach for handling these conversations: remain friendly and let the parent's frustration play out without matching it, listen fully without interrupting or countering every point, and then give a direct, honest, unapologetic explanation of why consistent accountability protects every student's right to learn, including the parent's own child. He provides a sample script for delivering this explanation and suggests closing with something genuinely positive about the child. Linsin insists teachers must remain equally consistent with parents as with students, standing firm even if the parent remains unsatisfied, since the teacher's job is to protect every student's learning environment—including from interference by parents themselves.
points: Parents increasingly complain not about the misbehavior itself but about the fact that a consequence was given at all.
The recommended three-step response is: stay friendly, listen fully without interrupting, then explain the reasoning directly and honestly.
A sample script frames accountability as protecting every student's right to learn, including the complaining parent's own child.
Ending the conversation with a genuine positive comment about the child helps close the interaction constructively.
Teachers must apply the same consistency to parents that they apply to students, holding firm even if a parent remains dissatisfied.
quotes: They don’t like the idea of them in time-out or having lunch detention or any other mode of accountability.
Now, it’s important to mention that parents who complain about accountability are often just frustrated that everything isn’t going as swimmingly for their child as they’d like.
Simple friendliness (classiness) will help diffuse their frustration and send the message that you’re competent, professional, and someone they can trust.

Every student in this classroom has the right to learn and enjoy school without interference, including yours, and it’s my job to protect that right by enforcing a consequence, as stated in our classroom management plan, every time a student breaks a rule.
Just as you’re consistent with your students, you must be equally consistent with parents.
You're paid to make decisions that are best for students, first and foremost, that protect their freedom to learn in a safe, peaceful, disruption-free, bully-free environment.
